According to Mark Gurman's latest Power On newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering making several changes to its App Store. The goal? To boost the potential revenue it brings in.

Apple's plans for App Store changes are not yet clear. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," with the effort being driven primarily by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Services SVP Eddy Cue.

This effort is reportedly one of the reasons veteran Phil Schiller left Apple last week. Schiller stepped down as SVP of Marketing in 2020 and transitioned to the role of Apple Fellow, where part of his responsibilities included overseeing the App Store. Schiller was not in favor of the idea:

There are many ways Apple could improve App Store margins. It could, for instance, eliminate its human app review process — an expensive one with questionable efficacy in an age of automated coding. Further automating review would likely upset users, but it would undoubtedly save money.

It could also raise its developer membership fee, which is currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers spend $200 per month on subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, you could argue Apple is well-positioned to raise prices without pushback. The company could also charge larger developers subscription fees based on traffic, passing on some of the costs of its infrastructure.

What the result will be remains to be seen, but I'm very much looking forward to seeing what these changes ultimately become.
